claims.source: We want to highlight that not all intact cells in the WT strain reported here are persisters. A significant portion comprises 'viable but non-culturable' (VBNC) cells, and WT cells exhibit markedly higher VBNC levels than Δcrp and ΔcyaA strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claims.claim: Mutant strains associated with the TCA pathway, ETC, ATP synthesis, and mixed acid fermentation pathways exhibited reduced tolerance to both ampicillin and ofloxacin compared to the control E. coli K-12 BW25113 WT strain.
claims.source: However, the mutant strains exhibited reduced tolerance to both antibiotics compared to the control E. coli K-12 BW25113 WT strain, which was found to be largely associated with the TCA pathway (sucA, sucB, lpd, sucC, sucD, sdhA, sdhB, sdhC, sdhD, gltA, acnB, aceE, fumA, mdh and fumC), ETC (nuoB, nuoC, nuoI, nuoK, nuoM, and narV), ATP synthesis (atpA, atpB, atpC, atpD, atpE, and atpH), and mixed acid fermentation pathways (ldhA, fdhF, pta, adhE, and frdC) (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by high-throughput screening data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 4

claims.claim: Knockout strains for key genes associated with the TCA, ETC, and ATP synthase showed reduced antibiotic tolerance, consistent with omics data and screening outcomes.
claims.source: To ensure the reproducibility of our findings, we generated knockout strains for key genes associated with the TCA, ETC, ATP synthase, glycolysis, and pentose phosphate pathway (Figure 5F, see Supplementary file 5 for detailed description of genes). We then tested their antibiotic tolerance, and our results were consistent with the omics data and screening outcomes (Figure 5F), confirming the critical role of energy metabolism, specifically the TCA cycle, ETC, and ATP synthase, in bacterial persistence.
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claims.claim: The Crp/cAMP regulatory complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells.
claims.source: Through metabolomics, proteomics, and high-throughput screening of single-gene deletion strains, we substantiated that the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics, proteomics, and high-throughput screening data presented in the study

claims.claim: This respiratory state is vital for the survival of persister cells, as perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex or respiration significantly reduced persister phenotypes.
claims.source: This respiratory state is vital for the survival of persister cells, as perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex or respiration significantly reduced persister phenotypes, which may explain the previously reported decrease in antibiotic tolerance in E. coli cells cultured under anaerobic conditions (Orman and Brynildsen, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Orman and Brynildsen, 2015

claims.claim: An upregulation of anabolic metabolites and proteins associated with cell wall organization, cell cycle, and cell division was observed when the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex was perturbed.
claims.source: Notably, we observed an upregulation of anabolic metabolites and proteins when the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex was perturbed, particularly those associated with cell wall organization, cell cycle, and cell division, enhancing the ability of stationary-phase mutant cells to resume growth.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics and proteomics data

claims.claim: The global metabolic regulator Crp/cAMP redirects the metabolism of antibiotic-tolerant cells from anabolism to oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.source: Our results indicate that the global metabolic regulator Crp/cAMP redirects the metabolism of these antibiotic-tolerant cells from anabolism to oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics and proteomics data presented in the study

claims.claim: Persisters exhibit a reduced metabolic rate compared to rapidly growing exponential-phase cells, but their survival still relies on energy metabolism.
claims.source: Although our data demonstrates that persisters exhibit a reduced metabolic rate compared to rapidly growing exponential-phase cells, their survival still relies on energy metabolism.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolic assays and knockout screening data

claims.claim: Energy metabolism, specifically the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, electron transport chain (ETC), and ATP synthase, plays a critical role in sustaining persister levels within cell populations.
claims.source: Extensive genomic-level analyses of metabolomics, proteomics, and single-gene deletions consistently highlight the critical role of energy metabolism, specifically the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, electron transport chain (ETC), and ATP synthase, in sustaining persister levels within cell populations.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics, proteomics, and knockout screening data

results.result: The manuscript provides background on bacterial persisters and their clinical significance, contrasting traditional views of dormancy with recent evidence of metabolic heterogeneity. It also draws parallels to tumor cell metabolism, noting that non-proliferating tumorigenic persisters rely on energy metabolism rather than aerobic glycolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1–C7 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific context and motivation for the study, accurately representing the current state of knowledge regarding persister cells and metabolic reprogramming in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems.

results.result: Deletion of cyaA reduces intracellular cAMP, while deletion of crp increases cAMP due to negative feedback regulation. All three strains (WT, Δcrp, ΔcyaA) enter stationary phase around 5 hr, and cAMP levels increase in WT during the transition to stationary phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C8–C11 are supported by experimental data (Figures 1—figure supplements 1–4) and align with known regulatory mechanisms. The observed cAMP dynamics are consistent with the feedback regulation of the Crp/cAMP complex on cyaA expression, and growth curves confirm comparable entry into stationary phase.

results.result: WT cells show increased ampicillin and ofloxacin persisters in late stationary phase, which is absent in Δcrp and ΔcyaA mutants. Complementation with crp restores persister levels. Gentamicin eliminates all persisters in all strains. The Crp/cAMP effect on persistence is also observed in the HipA7 background.
results.evaluation: Claims C12–C15 are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 1 and supplements). The complementation experiment (C13) provides genetic validation. The gentamicin result (C14) is consistent across strains and conditions. The HipA7 data (C15) extend the findings to a high-persister background, strengthening the conclusion that Crp/cAMP regulates persistence.

results.result: Metabolomics analysis reveals that WT cells in late stationary phase maintain energy metabolism while downregulating anabolic pathways. Disruption of the Crp/cAMP complex leads to downregulation of energy metabolism and upregulation of anabolic metabolites.
results.evaluation: Claims C16–C18 are supported by untargeted metabolomics data (Figure 2). Hierarchical clustering confirms reproducibility (C16). Pathway enrichment analysis supports the metabolic shifts described (C17, C18). The use of multiple biological replicates and appropriate statistical methods strengthens these findings.

results.result: Proteomics analysis shows that Δcrp mutants upregulate anabolic pathways (cell wall, cell cycle, division) and downregulate energy metabolism pathways (TCA cycle, ETC, glycolysis). Key TCA cycle and ETC proteins are specifically downregulated in the mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C19–C22 are supported by proteomics data (Figure 3 and supplement). Hierarchical clustering confirms consistency (C19). STRING pathway enrichment analysis identifies upregulated (C20) and downregulated (C21) pathways. Specific proteins involved in energy metabolism are identified (C22), providing molecular-level validation of the metabolomics findings.

results.result: WT cells in late stationary phase contain a non-dividing subpopulation absent in mutants. WT exhibits a longer lag phase and slower initial growth compared to mutants, while mutants show increased doubling time in exponential phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C23–C26 are supported by flow cytometry data using an mCherry dilution assay (Figure 4). The presence of non-dividing cells in WT but not mutants (C23, C24) correlates with persister levels. Growth kinetics (C25, C26) are consistent with the metabolic states inferred from omics data.

results.result: WT cells show higher SQR promoter activity and redox activity than mutants in stationary phase. Ampicillin-tolerant WT cells maintain elevated RSG levels, indicating active energy metabolism. WT exhibits higher VBNC levels than mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C27–C30 are supported by reporter assays (C27, Figure 5A), RSG dye assays (C28, C29, Figure 5B, D), and VBNC quantification (C30, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). These functional assays validate the omics findings and demonstrate that persister cells maintain metabolic activity. The distinction between persisters and VBNC cells is appropriately noted.

results.result: High-throughput screening of the Keio collection and validation with newly generated knockouts confirm that mutations in TCA cycle, ETC, ATP synthase, and fermentation pathways reduce antibiotic tolerance, while glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathway deletions do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C31–C32 are supported by screening data (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 4) and validation experiments (Figure 5F). The authors appropriately acknowledge potential errors in the Keio collection and validate key findings with independently generated knockouts. The consistency between screening and validation strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The Crp/cAMP complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells. This respiratory state is essential for persister survival. Persisters exhibit reduced but active energy metabolism compared to exponential-phase cells, with the TCA cycle, ETC, and ATP synthase playing critical roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C33–C38 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating findings from metabolomics, proteomics, and genetic screens. These claims are well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence (C33, C36, C38). The functional importance is demonstrated by genetic perturbations (C34). The upregulation of anabolic pathways in mutants (C35) and the reduced but active metabolism of persisters (C37) are supported by the data presented.

results.result: The authors characterized cAMP levels and growth dynamics in WT, Δcrp, and ΔcyaA strains. Deletion of cyaA reduced cAMP concentration as expected, while Δcrp showed increased cAMP, attributed to negative feedback regulation. All strains entered stationary phase around 5 hours, with cAMP levels increasing in WT during this transition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these basic characterization experiments. The reviewer noted 'there is no tested mechanisms explaining why the deletion of cyaA has an opposite effect on cAMP concentration compared to crp deletion,' acknowledging the observation while noting the mechanism was not experimentally validated. The data themselves are accepted as reproducible.

results.result: The WT strain showed marked increases in ampicillin- and ofloxacin-persister cells during late stationary phase, which were absent in Δcrp and ΔcyaA mutants. Complementation with crp restored persister levels, and gentamicin eliminated all tolerant cells. Similar effects were observed in the HipA7 background.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated that 'the data presented by the authors convincingly demonstrate that the deletion of two key genes that are part of the Crp/cAMP complex (i.e. crp and cyaA) leads to a significant decrease in the number of E. coli' persisters. The complementation and HipA7 validation experiments were noted as strengthening the findings.

results.result: Metabolomics analysis revealed that WT cells in late stationary phase maintain energy metabolism while downregulating anabolic pathways. Perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex led to downregulation of energy metabolism and upregulation of anabolic metabolites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'excellent understanding and presentation of the biochemical mechanisms underpinning bacterial physiology via an integrated genomic, metabolomic and proteomic screening.' They confirmed that 'the data presented also demonstrate that deletion of the crp gene leads to an overall decrease in energy metabolism and an overall increase in anabolic metabolism at the population level.'

results.result: Proteomics analysis showed that Δcrp mutants upregulated pathways associated with anabolic metabolism, cell wall organization, and cell division, while downregulating energy metabolism pathways including TCA cycle, glycolysis, and respiratory processes. Specific TCA cycle and ETC proteins were identified as downregulated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers commended the 'excellent use of replication and ensuring reproducibility' and the integrated approach. The proteomics findings were accepted as part of the convincing demonstration that Crp/cAMP regulates the metabolic shift. No concerns were raised about the pathway enrichment analysis or specific protein identifications.

results.result: Flow cytometry revealed a non-dividing subpopulation in WT late stationary phase cultures that was absent in mutant strains. WT cells showed slower initial growth and prolonged lag phase compared to mutants, while mutants had shorter lag phases but increased doubling times in exponential phase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'the authors convincingly show that the persisters they investigated are non-growing.' The flow cytometry data demonstrating non-dividing subpopulations and differential growth kinetics were accepted without critique, supporting the characterization of persister phenotypes.

results.result: Reporter assays and redox activity measurements showed upregulated succinate dehydrogenase (SQR) promoter activity and higher, more heterogeneous redox activities in WT compared to mutants. Ampicillin-tolerant WT cells maintained elevated redox activity. WT cells also exhibited markedly higher VBNC levels than mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers confirmed that the authors 'convincingly show that the persisters they investigated are non-growing and have a higher redox activity.' The redox activity data were accepted as validating the metabolomics and proteomics findings. The acknowledgment of VBNC cells was noted as appropriate transparency.

results.result: High-throughput screening of single-gene deletion mutants and validation with knockout strains demonstrated that genes associated with TCA cycle, ETC, ATP synthesis, and mixed acid fermentation pathways are critical for antibiotic tolerance. Knockout strains for key TCA, ETC, and ATP synthase genes showed reduced tolerance consistent with omics data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'the authors convincingly show that...the deletion of key genes involved in energy metabolism leads to a decrease in the number of persisters.' The screening approach and validation experiments were praised as part of the 'excellent understanding and presentation of the biochemical mechanisms' and the 'solid' evidence supporting the claims.

results.result: The authors conclude that the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells, and that this respiratory state is vital for persister survival. Energy metabolism (TCA cycle, ETC, ATP synthase) plays a critical role in sustaining persister levels, with persisters exhibiting reduced but active metabolism compared to exponential-phase cells.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found the overall evidence 'solid' and 'convincing,' they explicitly noted a critical limitation: 'Metabolomics, proteomics and metabolic activity data are obtained at the whole population level rather than at the level of the persister sub-population.' The authors acknowledged this caveat, and reviewers stated the data 'should be considered with caution.' This creates uncertainty about whether the metabolic state described truly characterizes persisters specifically or the broader stationary-phase population.

comparisons.comparison: OpenEval evaluated claims C1-C7 regarding scientific context and literature citations as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation was found for these background/introduction claims.

Both evaluate claims C8-C11 regarding cAMP dynamics and growth curves as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistency with known regulatory mechanisms. Peer reviewers accepted the data as reproducible while noting the mechanism explaining opposite effects of cyaA vs crp deletion was not experimentally validated.

Both evaluate claims C12-C15 regarding Crp/cAMP regulation of persistence as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement that the data convincingly demonstrate deletion of crp and cyaA leads to decreased persisters, with complementation and HipA7 experiments strengthening the findings.

Both evaluate claims C16-C18 regarding metabolomics findings as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement on the quality of the integrated approach and the demonstration that crp deletion leads to decreased energy metabolism and increased anabolic metabolism at the population level.

Both evaluate claims C19-C22 regarding proteomics data as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement on the quality of replication, reproducibility, and the integrated approach validating metabolic shifts at the molecular level.

Both evaluate claims C23-C26 regarding flow cytometry and non-dividing cells as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement that the data convincingly show persisters are non-growing, with differential growth kinetics consistent with inferred metabolic states.

Both evaluate claims C27-C30 regarding metabolic activity assays as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement that the data convincingly demonstrate persisters are non-growing with higher redox activity, validating omics findings and appropriately distinguishing VBNC cells.

Both evaluate claims C31-C32 regarding genetic screening as SUPPORTED. Complete agreement on the quality of the screening approach and validation experiments demonstrating that deletion of energy metabolism genes decreases persister numbers.

Critical disagreement on claims C33-C38 regarding main conclusions. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on convergence of multiple lines of evidence. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting that metabolomics, proteomics, and metabolic activity data are from whole populations rather than persister subpopulations specifically, requiring caution in interpretation.
